\begin{proof}
The elements of $(1+i)$ are precisely the Gaussian integers whose real and imaginary parts have the same parity. In fact,
\[
(1+i)(u+vi)=(u-v)+(u+v)i,
\]
whose two coordinates have the same parity; conversely, if $a\equiv b\pmod2$, taking $u=(a+b)/2$ and $v=(b-a)/2$ gives
\[
(1+i)(u+vi)=a+bi.
\]
Hence, for every $a+bi$, either $a+bi\in(1+i)$ or $a-1+bi\in(1+i)$. Thus there are at most two cosets. They are distinct since $1\notin(1+i)$, so the quotient has exactly two elements. Its nonzero element is the class of $1$, which is its own multiplicative identity; consequently every nonzero element is invertible. Therefore $\mathbb Z[i]/(1+i)$ is a field of order $2$.
\end{proof}
